profiles.meeting_scenario: CodeHinter's team is holding a troubleshooting meeting two days before a new undergraduate pilot session after noticing an odd pattern in the second design iteration: students in the recent pilot appeared to rely heavily on the error localization panel, full-fix requests spiked in some sessions, and the dashboard shows a drop in successful semantic-error resolution for 'last week's pilot.' The meeting is between the applied ML lead who oversaw the study design and the platform engineer who owns the hinting/telemetry pipeline. Their agenda is to determine whether the problem is a real product regression, a configuration or logging issue, or an artifact of a specific pilot run, and to decide what they will patch or verify before the next cohort starts. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan and an agreed immediate mitigation for the upcoming pilot.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: LLM-assisted programming tools, novice debugging behavior, study instrumentation
members.background: Maya is a faculty-affiliated research lead who designed CodeHinter's second iteration and analyzes how students use localization, explanation, and repair features during pilot studies.
members.private_state: She wants to protect the validity of the pilot findings and is worried that a backend or UI change may have quietly altered how much agency students had during debugging, which could undermine the interpretation of the study.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'last week's pilot,' they mean the scheduled CS1 lab sections that used the standard semantic-error worksheet, not the smaller make-up usability sessions.
When the team says the system was on 'fallback,' that means students only got the non-generative localization workflow because the LLM layer was effectively unavailable.
A problem is 'fixed' only if the interaction pattern again supports active engagement, such as students investigating localized errors before accepting a solution.
Replaying a session should mean using the archived client event stream from the original student run so the team can inspect the exact behavior students experienced.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Backend services, feature flags, observability, educational tooling deployments
members.background: Leo maintains the CodeHinter hint service, prompt-routing layer, telemetry dashboards, and staging environment used to validate releases before classroom pilots.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid an unnecessary rollback before Thursday and suspects the issue is a configuration or dashboard interpretation problem rather than a true product failure.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'last week's pilot,' they mean the latest sessions included in the default telemetry dashboard view, which currently bundles the Friday make-up section with the main pilot runs.
When the team says the system hit 'fallback,' that means requests were served by the older cached v1 prompt template rather than the newest multi-step LLM hint flow.
A problem is 'fixed' once the service behaves operationally normally again, especially no error banner, no dropped requests, and acceptable latency on the hint endpoint.
Replaying a session means reproducing the issue in staging with the same assignment package and feature flags against the current backend, because that is the fastest way to validate a root cause.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'last week's pilot' and 'the affected sessions' as though they mean the same set of students.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the two scheduled Wednesday CS1 lab sections that used the linked-list semantic-error assignment in the formal second-iteration study.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the dashboard's latest combined slice, which also includes the Friday make-up usability session with a smaller array-index assignment and different traffic pattern.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe there was only one relevant recent pilot bundle, and because the dashboard label and calendar shorthand feel obvious internally, neither thinks to restate the exact session IDs or assignment names.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say students were 'on fallback' for a noticeable portion of the run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the generative hinting layer was effectively absent, so students mainly experienced localization-only support and lost the intended guided-debugging flow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the backend routed requests to the legacy cached v1 prompt template, which still returns AI hints but skips the newer multi-step prompting pipeline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Inside the team, 'fallback' is treated as routine operational shorthand, and both versions still produce some form of hinting, so surface behavior seems close enough that neither notices the semantic mismatch.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to have the issue 'fixed' before Thursday
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they need the issue 'fixed' or the system 'stable' before the next cohort.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 will consider it fixed only if student behavior again reflects active engagement, such as explanation requests and stepwise debugging patterns returning to normal relative to the second-iteration design goals.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 will consider it fixed once the service no longer throws visible errors, stays under the target p95 latency threshold, and stops dropping hint requests.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a troubleshooting meeting, 'fixed' and 'stable' sound like unremarkable shared goals; both assume the other naturally includes their own criterion, so the difference remains hidden behind cooperative planning language.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'replay one of the bad sessions' to verify the root cause.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a reconstruction from archived client-side interaction logs and original timestamps so they can inspect the precise user experience from the study run.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to reproduce the issue in staging using the same assignment bundle and copied feature flags against the current service stack.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Replay sounds like a standard debugging step, and both methods are common in this team; because each method is reasonable and no one asks for the mechanics, they leave with different next steps while feeling aligned.

turns.inner_thought: The Wednesday CS1 lab sections from the formal second-iteration study looked wrong to me. On the linked-list semantic-error worksheet, students should have been using localization to orient, then requesting explanations, then attempting repairs. Instead, they seemed to camp in localization and jump to full fixes more often, and the semantic-error resolution rate dipped. If something in the backend or UI quietly reduced agency during those scheduled lab runs, the pilot findings get much harder to interpret.
turns.utterance: I want to start with last week's pilot, because the pattern looked off. Students leaned much more heavily on the localization panel than I expected, and the semantic-error resolution rate for the affected sessions came in lower than our second-iteration baseline.

turns.inner_thought: I saw the same overall drop in the dashboard slice for the recent sessions, including the Friday make-up traffic. What stood out on my side was that the hint service spent a noticeable chunk of those runs on fallback. To me that means the router wasn't using the newest multi-step prompt flow and was serving the older cached v1 prompt template instead. That's not ideal, but it's not the same as the system being unavailable.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I was looking at the affected sessions too, and one thing that jumped out is that the service was on fallback for a noticeable portion of the run. So I do think there was something unusual happening during last week's pilot.

turns.inner_thought: That fits my fear: if they were on fallback, then the generative layer was effectively absent and students were basically left with localization without the intended guided-debugging support. That would absolutely thin out explanation-seeking and push students toward either stalling or asking for a full fix too early. If that's what happened in the Wednesday sections, I may need to treat those data differently.
turns.utterance: That would line up with what I was seeing behaviorally. If students were on fallback for that stretch, the guided debugging flow would have felt a lot thinner, and that could easily push them toward localization without the same level of active engagement.

turns.inner_thought: I don't think fallback would have stripped hints away; the legacy template still returns usable hints, just without the newer orchestration. So maybe the bigger issue was slow responses or timeout behavior making the experience feel degraded. If I can get latency under control, I can probably avoid any rollback and keep Thursday on track.
turns.utterance: Possibly, although fallback shouldn't have removed hints entirely. The older path still answers, and usually pretty fast, so I'm wondering whether latency was the bigger culprit here rather than capability. If the service was sluggish enough, that could explain a lot of what you saw.

turns.inner_thought: I'm talking about the Wednesday linked-list study sessions, not the smaller make-up group. Those are the runs I need to protect. And 'fixed before Thursday' doesn't just mean the endpoint behaves; it means student interaction patterns look like the second-iteration design again—localization as an entry point, explanations in the middle, repair decisions with real participation. If that behavior doesn't come back, I still won't trust the next cohort data.
turns.utterance: Right, and for me the key thing is that in last week's pilot, especially in the Wednesday run, the system needs to be fixed before Thursday in a way that restores the intended debugging behavior. I don't just want the symptom to go away; I want the student flow to look like what we designed for.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, priority is getting the platform stable before Thursday. I can tighten the timeout, watch p95 on the hint endpoint, and make sure we're not dropping requests or surfacing banners. If the service is healthy and responsive again, that should count as fixed enough to proceed with the next cohort without a rollback.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On my side, I can get it stable before Thursday by tightening the timeout behavior and checking the p95 on the hint endpoint. If we stop the slowdowns and keep requests flowing cleanly, we should be in much better shape for the next cohort.

turns.inner_thought: I need to inspect the actual archived client event stream from one of those Wednesday student runs. That's the only way to see exactly when they stopped requesting explanations, whether the UI state changed, and whether they were effectively being funneled into full fixes. A synthetic repro won't tell me what the student actually experienced during the pilot.
turns.utterance: Could we replay one of the bad sessions before we make any bigger call? I'd really like to inspect exactly where students stopped asking for explanations and started shifting straight to fixes.

turns.inner_thought: Sure, easiest path is to reproduce it in staging with the same assignment package and feature flags, then test whether the timeout adjustment clears it. That'll give me a quick read on root cause this afternoon without waiting on log archaeology. If I can make the repro disappear in staging, that's probably enough evidence that the issue is operational and patchable.
turns.utterance: Yes, let's do that. I can replay one of the bad sessions in staging after lunch with the same assignment package and feature flags, and then we can see whether the timeout change removes the issue.

turns.inner_thought: If the replay of an actual pilot run shows the same pattern, I don't necessarily want to touch the new UI right away, because that would confound things further. I mainly want to verify that students are using localization as a starting point again rather than getting stranded there. If explanation requests and stepwise debugging recover, then I'd be more comfortable saying the issue is truly fixed for study purposes.
turns.utterance: Good. And if the replay confirms the pattern from last week's pilot, my preference is to keep the new UI for now but verify that students are using localization as a starting point again rather than a dead end. That's the behavior I want us to recover before Thursday.

turns.inner_thought: I'll review the dashboard slice for the recent sessions, including the make-up group, patch the fallback path so it routes cleanly, and confirm the service is healthy. Once latency and dropped requests look normal, I'll tell Maya we're stable for Thursday. I still think this is more likely config or observability than a true product regression.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll review the pilot dashboard slice again, patch the fallback behavior, and report back once the system looks stable for the next cohort.
